questions.q_en:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

The chief engineer, unlike his assistants and the site supervisors, ________ extremely disappointed when he realized that the construction ________ been delayed indefinitely.
questions.q_hi:

The chief engineer, unlike his assistants and the site supervisors, ________ extremely disappointed when he realized that the construction ________ been delayed indefinitely.
options_en: were / have

were / has
was / has
options_hi: were / have

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (D)- The blanks should be filled with "was" and "has".

Rule/Concept: First Subject Priority When two subjects are joined by words like "unlike," "together with," "besides," "rather than," or "except," the verb must always agree with the first subject. The subsequent nouns (assistants/supervisors) are merely sub-qualifiers.

Logic Breakdown:

The Main Subject: The sentence is built around "The chief engineer" (Singular).

The Qualifier: "unlike his assistants and the site supervisors" is extra information. Even though it contains plural nouns, it does not make the subject plural.

Blank 1 (Verb): Since the chief engineer is singular, we must use "was." This eliminates options (A) and (C).

Blank 2 (Tense): The word "construction" is also singular, requiring the singular helping verb "has" to complete the "has been delayed" structure. This eliminates option (B).

Agreement: "The chief engineer (Singular) ... was (Singular) ... construction (Singular) ... has (Singular)."

Correct Sentence: The chief engineer... was extremely disappointed... construction has been delayed...

options_hi: The legal department was alarmed to find that multiple
summons had been delivered to the corporate office while
the executive board was away on an international retreat.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “summons” with “summonses”.

Rule / Concept: Singular and Plural of 'Summons

Summons is a singular countable noun, even though it ends in 's'. Because it is singular, it follows the standard rule for nouns ending in 's' when becoming plural: you must add -es.

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the adjective "multiple" indicates a plural quantity. The word "summons" is singular. To match the plural requirement of "multiple," the word must be converted to its plural form, which is summonses. Using "summons" in a plural context is a common error because it already "looks" plural due to the terminal 's'.

Summons (singular) ✅

Summonses (plural) ✅

questions.q_en:
Select the passive form of the given sentence.

The employee got promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
questions.q_hi:
Select the passive form of the given sentence.

The employee got promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
options_en: The employee was promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
The employee had promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
The employee has got been promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
The employee got being promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
options_hi: The employee was promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
The employee had promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
The employee has got been promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
The employee got being promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A)

📌 Rule / Concept: Get-Passive and Its Standard Passive Equivalent

The structure “get + V³” is known as the get-passive. It is commonly used in informal English and often emphasizes that the subject was affected by the action. However, in formal written English (and in competitive exams), the standard passive form uses:

Subject + be (appropriate tense) + V³

Thus, “got promoted” corresponds to “was promoted” in standard passive structure.

💢 Application to the Given Question - Here, “got promoted” is already passive in meaning (get-passive). To convert it into the standard passive structure, replace “got” with the correct form of “be” in the same tense.

Since “got” is simple past, the correct passive form becomes:

The employee was promoted after demonstrating exceptional leadership skills.

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

“Get + V³” is already passive in meaning but informal. In exams, prefer “be + V³.” Match the tense correctly when replacing “got” with “was/were.” This structure is frequently tested to check conceptual clarity about passive meaning versus passive form.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (D)

📌 Rule / Concept: Present Perfect Continuous – No Passive Form

The active structure of Present Perfect Continuous is:
Subject + has/have + been + V-ing + Object

There is no standard passive form of Present Perfect Continuous in formal English. Constructions like “has been being evaluated” are grammatically possible in theory but are considered awkward, unnatural, and not accepted in competitive exam standards such as SSC or Banking. Therefore, in exam-oriented grammar, this tense does not have a valid passive transformation.

The verb phrase “has been evaluating” is in Present Perfect Continuous tense. Since this tense does not form a standard passive construction, options attempting structures like “has been being evaluated” are incorrect. Hence, the only correct answer is that no passive form is possible.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: The security guard claimed that he
distinctly heard someone to open the
heavy iron gate after midnight.
No Error
options_hi: The security guard claimed that he
distinctly heard someone to open the
heavy iron gate after midnight.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “to open” with “open”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Bare Infinitives after Verbs of Perception

Use bare infinitive after these verbs- Let, Bid, Make, See, Notice, Feel, Hear, Smell, have, Watch, Help Etc.

Verbs of perception—such as see, hear, watch, feel, notice, and observe—follow a specific pattern when they take an object. When you see or hear the entire action from start to finish, you must use a Bare Infinitive (V1 without "to").

💢 Application to the Given Question

"...heard someone to open the heavy iron gate..."

In this sentence, the verb of perception is "heard" and the object is "someone." According to the rule, the following action (opening the gate) must be in the base form. The use of "to open" is grammatically incorrect in this structure. It should be "open" (to imply the whole action was heard) or "opening" (to imply the action was heard while in progress).

Corrected Sentence

The security guard claimed that he distinctly heard someone open the heavy iron gate after midnight.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅ I saw her dance at the concert. (I saw the whole performance)

Example 2 ✅ We felt the house shake during the blast.

Example 3 ✅ Did you notice him leave the room?

Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1 ❌ I heard him to sing a song.

Wrong example 2 ❌ They watched the ship to disappear into the mist.

be present at the upcoming annual general meeting to discuss the fiscal deficit
and that no one is allowed to leave the premises until a consensus is reached.
No Error
options_hi: The chairperson of the high-level committee insisted that every member of the advisory board

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C).

Replace “is” with “be”.

📌 Rule / Concept: The Mandative Present Subjunctive Mood

Certain verbs (insist, suggest, demand, recommend, mandate) or adjectives (essential, vital, important) followed by the conjunction that require the base form of the verb (the subjunctive mood) in the following clause. This base form remains constant regardless of the tense of the main verb or the number/person of the subject.

💢 Application to the Given Question - The main verb of the sentence is insisted. This insistence governs two parallel clauses:

  1. "...that every member... be present" (Correctly used subjunctive).

  2. "...that no one is allowed..." (Incorrectly used indicative).

Because the chairperson is still "insisting" on this second condition, the verb must also be in the base form (be) rather than the indicative form (is).

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1 ✅ - The judge ordered that the defendant remain in custody.

Example 2 ✅ - It is essential that he arrive on time for the hearing.

Example 3 ✅- I suggest that she not be told about the surprise yet.

questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: Each employee working across the departments of finance, audit, and regulatory compliance
are expected to attend the mandatory briefing scheduled before the
the commencement of the annual inspection and external review process.
No error
options_hi: Each employee working across the departments of finance, audit, and regulatory compliance
are expected to attend the mandatory briefing scheduled before the
the commencement of the annual inspection and external review process.
No error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “are expected” with “is expected”.

Rule / Concept: Each vs Every

Each is used for individual items in a group (2 or more) and always takes a singular verb.

Every is used for all items collectively (more than two) and also takes a singular verb.

Plural verbs with “Each” or “Every” are incorrect.

Application to the Given Question -

“Each employee … are expected to attend…”

Each employee → refers to individual employees one by one.

Therefore, the verb must be singular: “is expected” instead of “are expected”.

Corrected Sentence - Each employee working across the departments of finance, audit, and regulatory compliance is expected to attend the mandatory briefing scheduled before the commencement of the annual inspection and external review process.

More Examples for Clarity -

Each student in the class is required to submit the assignment by Monday.

Every member of the team has contributed to the project report.

Each of the candidates was informed about the interview schedule individually.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips -

Always check the subject-verb agreement with Each/Every.

Look for long modifiers—they do not change the singular nature of the subject.

SSC frequently tests subtle errors in long, official-sounding sentences.

questions.q_en:
Identify the type of the highlighted non-finite phrase.

Having completed the presentation successfully, the senior analyst submitted the final report to the management.
questions.q_hi:
Identify the type of the highlighted non-finite phrase.

Having completed the presentation successfully, the senior analyst submitted the final report to the management.
options_en: Infinitive Phrase
Gerund Phrase
Participial Phrase
Noun Phrase
options_hi: Infinitive Phrase
Gerund Phrase
Participial Phrase
Noun Phrase
questions.solution_en:
Answer: C) Participial Phrase

Explanation: A participial phrase begins with a participle and functions as an adjective.

The highlighted phrase begins with:

“Having completed” which is a participle form.

The phrase describes the “senior analyst.”

Which analyst? → analyst having completed the presentation successfully

Therefore, it is a participial phrase.

Why other options are incorrect:

A) An infinitive phrase begins with “to + verb.”

B) A gerund phrase functions as a noun.

D) A noun phrase functions as a noun and does not begin with a participle.

has roused deep suspicion among the federal investigators, who now believe
that an internal whistleblower might be involved in the sophisticated corporate espionage.
No Error
options_hi: The mysterious disappearance of the confidential documents from the high-security vault

No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “roused” with “aroused”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Rouse vs. Arouse -

While both verbs deal with "waking" or "stirring," they are used in distinct contexts:

Rouse: Primarily refers to waking someone from sleep, unconsciousness, or physical inactivity. It is often used for a physical or literal awakening (e.g., "The alarm roused him from sleep").

Arouse: Primarily refers to stimulating feelings, emotions, suspicions, or physiological responses. It deals with abstract concepts like curiosity, interest, or anger (e.g., "The news aroused his curiosity").

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the object is "suspicion," which is an emotion or a mental state. You do not physically wake suspicion from a nap; you stimulate or evoke it. Therefore, the abstract verb aroused is the grammatically correct choice here.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1: We managed to rouse the dog from its deep slumber.

Example 2: The politician's controversial remarks aroused a great deal of anger.

Example 3: It was difficult to rouse the troops after the exhausting march.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: It is I who is
responsible for managing the
daily operations of this firm.
No Error
options_hi: It is I who is
responsible for managing the
daily operations of this firm.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A).

Replace “is” with “am”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Relative Pronoun Antecedent Agreement -

When a sentence follows the structure "It is [Pronoun] + who/that," the verb in the relative clause must agree with the antecedent (the noun or pronoun that comes immediately before who/that).

Even though "It" is the subject of the first part of the sentence, the word "who" is actually acting as the subject for the second part. Since "who" is representing "I", it must take the verb form that "I" would naturally take.

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the relative pronoun is "who." Its antecedent is "I." Now, ask yourself: would you ever say "I is responsible"? No. You would say "I am responsible." Because "who" stands in for "I", the verb following it must be "am". Using "is" is a common error because "is" sounds correct following the third-person "who," but grammatically, it must match the person and number of the antecedent.

More Examples for Clarity

questions.solution_en:
Rule / Concept: Differ from vs. Differ on

In competitive exams, "Differ" is a high-frequency verb that changes its preposition based on whether you are comparing attributes or discussing opinions:

Example: My car differs from yours in color.

Example: I differ from you on this matter.

Example: We differ on the question of taxation.

Application to the Given Question

"...design will significantly differ from the original blueprint, causing the architects to differ from the lead engineer differ on the feasibility..."

First Blank: Comparing two objects (New design vs. Blueprint). This is a physical/structural dissimilarity, so "from" is used.

Second Blank: Expressing disagreement with a person (The lead engineer). To disagree with a person is to "differ from" them.

Third Blank: Identifying the specific topic of disagreement (The feasibility of using glass). This is the matter/issue at hand, requiring "on".

Rule/Concept: Fractions and Percentages (The "Of" Rule) When a sentence starts with a percentage (e.g., 90%), a fraction (e.g., one-third), or a portion (e.g., some, all, most), the verb agrees with the noun following the word "of".

Logic Breakdown:

The Noun after "of": In this sentence, the noun is "students" (Plural Countable Noun).

Rule/Concept: Lest... should (Fixed Conjunction Pair) –

In English grammar, the conjunction "Lest" is used to express the idea of "to avoid the risk of" or "for fear that." It has a very specific grammatical requirement: it is almost always followed by the modal verb "should". Even though the sentence may imply a future possibility or a different modal sense (like may or might), "should" is the only grammatically correct companion for "lest" in formal exams.

More Examples for Clarity -

  1. Walk carefully lest you should fall.

  2. He studied hard lest he should fail the examination.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips -

  1. Lest Check: 90% of 'Should' questions in SSC revolve around the 'Lest...should' pair.

  2. Inversion Recognition: If a sentence starts with a blank and ends with a comma before a command/request, check if 'Should' (meaning 'If') fits.

  3. Probability: Use 'Should' when you are saying "I expect this to happen."

Rule / Concept: Possessive Case of Celestial Bodies

While we generally avoid using the apostrophe 's with inanimate objects (e.g., we say "the legs of the table," not "the table's legs"), certain nouns are treated as exceptions due to their dignity, personification, or astronomical significance.

Nouns representing celestial bodies—such as the Earth, Sun, Moon, and Planets—are traditionally used with the possessive 's when referring to their properties, movements, or influences.

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, "gravitational changes" belong to the "Earth." Since Earth is a celestial body, it requires the possessive form to show this relationship. Leaving it as "earth" makes it a noun adjunct that sounds incomplete or ungrammatical in formal writing. Adding the apostrophe and 's' correctly identifies the gravity as a property belonging to our planet.

questions.q_hi:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

Dev asked her brother why he had not gone there the day before.
options_en: Dev said to her brother, "Why you did not go here yesterday?"
Dev said to her brother, "Why did you not go here yesterday?"
Dev said to her brother, "Why didn't you go there yesterday?"
Dev said to her brother, "Why you did not go there the day before?"
options_hi: Dev said to her brother, "Why you did not go here yesterday?"
Dev said to her brother, "Why did you not go here yesterday?"
Dev said to her brother, "Why didn't you go there yesterday?"
Dev said to her brother, "Why you did not go there the day before?"
questions.solution_en:
The correct answer is Option B: Dev said to her brother, "Why did you not go here yesterday?"

  • The Tense Shift (Past Perfect to Simple Past): In the indirect speech, we have "had not gone" (Past Perfect). To revert to Direct Speech, we must move one step forward to the Simple Past: "did you not go".

  • The Place Shift (There to Here): In narration, "here" becomes "there". So, when reversing to Direct Speech, "there" must change back to "here". Option C and D fail this test.

  • The Time Shift (The Day Before to Yesterday): The phrase "the day before" is the indirect version of "yesterday". Option D fails this test.

  • The Sentence Structure: In a direct question, the auxiliary verb (did) must come before the subject (you). Option A is a "syntax trap" because it puts the subject first, which is only done in indirect speech.
